e: Plain English Words this page uses because the courts use them. Nothing here is special to this case. The paperwork How a case moves Pleas The tests in this case

N.Y. Sup. Ct., New York Cty., Part 32 · Ind. No. 75657‑24 · S.D.N.Y. · No. 1:25‑cr‑00176 People v. Mangione One killing, charged in three places at once: by New York, by the federal government, and by a county in Pennsylvania. For eighteen months the interesting question was which of them would go first, and New York won that argument. Then, three and a half weeks before the state murder trial was due to begin — and five months before his own federal trial — the defendant pleaded guilty to everything the federal government had left against him, with no agreement and nothing offered in return. New York’s double jeopardy statute is broader than the Fifth Amendment, and the plea is what gave it something to attach to. Whether the state may still try him for the same killing is now the only question left, and it is undecided. Indicted Dec 17, 2024 Before Carro, J. · Garnett, J. Pleaded Aug 14, 2026 Status Undecided

Prosecution The side bringing the charges The State of New York A criminal case in New York is brought in the name of the People, which just means the state. The lawyers are from the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office, which Alvin Bragg runs, because the killing happened in Manhattan. They aren’t the only ones who charged him. The federal government did too, and so did a county in Pennsylvania, where he was arrested. Background: Manhattan District Attorney

Defendant The person charged Computer science graduate He was 26 when he was arrested. He grew up outside Baltimore, Maryland, in a wealthy family whose businesses there include country clubs and a care home company. He finished top of his class at a private school in 2016, then took a bachelor’s and a master’s degree in computer science at the University of Pennsylvania. After that he worked remotely as a data engineer for a car-buying website and lived for a while in Hawaii, where he hurt his back. Background: Britannica

Notes Record reviewed through November 8, 2026 . Both cases are live: the federal one awaits sentence on December 18, and the state one awaits a decision on a motion both sides have now briefed. This page will be wrong in some particular within weeks, which is the condition of writing about a case while it is still happening.
How this was made, and what it leaves out

The federal case is built from its own docket, No. 1:25‑cr‑00176 (MMG), read in full through the archive of PACER filings. Every federal citation on this page is an ECF No. and can be pulled from that docket. The two January opinions are quoted from the filed text. The state indictment is quoted from the signed copy published by the District Attorney’s office, and the August 17 scheduling order from the copy filed in Part 32 — both in full, both short. The People’s October 9 response is quoted from the copy Courthouse News published. The two state decisions that matter most — the September 2025 omnibus decision and the May 2026 suppression decision — are summarized here from contemporaneous reporting of them, with one quoted passage from the first. That is a weaker chain than the rest of the page and is marked as such below.

The People answered the double jeopardy motion on October 9, 2026, and the defense replied at the end of the month. The Side by Side View sets the two side by side, each quoted from its own papers. The defense reply is quoted from the court-stamped copy LA Magazine published. New York County Supreme Court has no public docket of the kind PACER provides, so the state record here is not a complete list of filings in the way the federal one is. Where a state filing is described, it is because a copy or a reliable account of it is public — not because the docket was read end to end. Assume the state side is less complete than the federal side, because it is. The Pennsylvania case is noted once and then dropped. It has never been tried and nothing in it bears on the question this page is about.

Brian Thompson was fifty, and had a wife and two sons. The case is interesting for reasons of statutory construction, and a page organized around statutory construction can quietly turn a killing into a puzzle. He is named here every time the record names him, and the one thing nobody in any of these courtrooms has disputed since August 14, 2026, is how he died. One reading on this page is an inference rather than a fact: that the open plea was entered to trigger the state double jeopardy bar. Neither side has said so on the record. It is marked as an inference where it appears, and it is the only place this page reasons about motive.

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict. He has been convicted of two federal stalking offenses by his own plea and has not been tried for murder by anybody. The state counts are allegations and remain allegations, and the question of whether they can be tried at all is undecided by the only person who gets to decide it. Where the record does not reach, this page says so and stops.
The court’s numbered list of everything filed in a case. Entry 42 is the forty-second thing filed.
How a federal filing is cited: its docket number. A number after a dash, like 59-2, is an attachment to it — usually an exhibit.
The document a grand jury returns to start a felony prosecution. It lists the charges and nothing else; it is not evidence of anything.
One charged offense. An indictment with eleven counts charges eleven separate offenses, and a jury answers for each one separately.
A panel that hears the prosecution’s evidence in secret and decides whether there is enough to charge. It does not decide guilt.
The word-for-word record of a hearing. Cited by page and line, so 12:7 means page 12, line 7.
Filed with the court but kept off the public record. Both sides and the judge can read it; nobody else can.
The hearing where a defendant is formally told the charges and enters a plea to them.
A formal request that the court do something. The other side files an opposition or response; the moving side may then reply.
Keeping evidence out of a trial because of how it was obtained. The evidence may be entirely genuine; the question is only whether the police were entitled to get it that way.

A search of a detained person’s property to log what is in it, done to a standard procedure rather than to look for evidence. Lawful without a warrant, which is why the procedure itself gets litigated.
The caution police must give before questioning someone in custody. Answers given before it are generally inadmissible; answers to routine booking or safety questions generally are not affected.
The questioning of prospective jurors before a trial, to decide who sits on it.
An appeal taken in the middle of a case, before final judgment, usually only where a statute allows it.
An investigation by the probation office, ordered after conviction, that the judge reads before sentencing.

A lawyer experienced in death penalty cases, appointed at public expense whenever a federal case is capital. Required by statute, not discretionary — so the appointment arriving and being withdrawn marks when a case was and was not capital.
Which of two governments holding claims on the same defendant gets to deal with him first. It usually follows who arrested him.
Pennsylvania’s speedy-trial rule. It normally requires trial within a year of the complaint, but time a defendant is unavailable does not count against it.
A guilty plea entered with no agreement from the prosecution — no charge concessions, no sentencing recommendation. The defendant gives up the trial and keeps none of the usual consideration for it.
The usual arrangement: a plea in exchange for something, normally dropped charges or a position on sentence. There was none here.
The bar on being prosecuted twice for the same offense. New York’s statutory version is broader than the Fifth Amendment’s and reaches across sovereigns.
The doctrine that a state and the federal government are separate sovereigns, so a prosecution by each for the same conduct is not the same offense under the Fifth Amendment.

Conduct closely connected enough in time and purpose to count as one episode. New York’s double jeopardy statute works on transactions, not just on single acts — which is why the date on a count matters.
One of the separate things a prosecutor has to prove for a particular crime. If one is missing, the charge fails.

The section of New York’s Criminal Procedure Law that holds the state’s double jeopardy rule. Its second part bars a second prosecution over the same act or criminal transaction, and then lists the exceptions.
For these statutes, a felony that has as an element the use, attempted use, or threatened use of physical force against the person or property of another.
An offense that another, more serious charge is built on top of. If the predicate fails as a matter of law, the charge built on it fails with it.
A method that ignores what the defendant actually did and asks only whether the offense, as written, always requires force — judged by the least serious conduct the statute could cover.
The evidence put before the grand jury, taken at its best, could not establish an element of the charge. The count goes without any finding about whether the defendant did it.
A New York classification attaching to certain offenses committed with a loaded weapon. It restricts what sentence and what plea are available.

Where it stands Waiting on the third question. Both sides have filed, and the court has not ruled on the motion. If yes If yes If yes If no Either way The Fifth Amendment is not on this diagram, and that is the point of it. The constitutional claim does not branch — under dual sovereignty it simply fails, because two sovereigns prosecuting the same conduct are not prosecuting the same offense. Everything here runs on a New York statute that chose to be broader than the Constitution. And note what the third question asks of the People: that federal stalking and intentional murder be aimed at very different kinds of harm. The strongest authority for that proposition is the January ruling that stalking is not a crime of violence — the ruling that took the death penalty off the table.

The first question Yes for murder, since Aug 14, 2026 Double jeopardy is the rule that you can’t be prosecuted twice for the same thing, and New York has its own version written into state law. That law only does anything once there’s an earlier prosecution that has actually ended in something, like a conviction. So the first question is if there is one. He was charged over the same killing in more than one court. Two of them matter here, the federal government’s case and the State of New York’s. This card starts with the federal case, and it’s finished. On August 14, 2026, he pleaded guilty in federal court to two counts of stalking, each one for stalking that ended in a death. A count is one charged offense. A guilty plea is a conviction, the same as if a jury had found him guilty, and that conviction is what everything below hangs on. He is due to be sentenced on December 18, 2026, and each count carries up to life in prison. The defense tried the double jeopardy argument in May 2025 and lost, because back then the federal case was still going and nothing had ended. The guilty plea on August 14, 2026, changed that. A guilty plea is a conviction, so now there is an earlier prosecution, and the answer is yes. That yes is for the murder count. For the seven weapons counts, the prosecution says no. The federal case had two gun charges of its own, but the federal judge threw them out in January 2026, at the defense’s request, so by the time he pleaded guilty he wasn’t charged with them anymore. The defense says that doesn’t matter, because the case they were part of still ended in a guilty plea. The judge hasn’t decided that one either.
Was it the same act, or the same criminal transaction?
New York’s counts three through ten

The second question Not in dispute This card starts with the New York case, and it’s the one in question. The indictment, which is the document that lists the charges, started out with eleven counts. A judge threw out the first two, the terrorism ones, in September 2025. Counts three through ten are what’s left from the day of the shooting. That’s one count of second-degree murder and seven weapons counts. Every one of them is dated on or about December 4, 2024, the same morning the federal case was about. That shared date is why the defense has asked the court to dismiss all eight. The second question is if both cases are about the same thing. Under the US Constitution this wouldn’t even be asked. The federal government and a state count as two separate governments, or sovereigns, and the Constitution lets each one prosecute the same conduct. New York’s own law is stricter. It counts a federal prosecution too, as long as both cases come out of the same act or the same criminal transaction, which basically means one connected episode. That stricter state law is the only reason this fight exists. And the answer here isn’t really in dispute. Both cases are about one defendant, one victim, one street and one morning.
Does an exception in CPL 40.20(2) apply?

The case is here The third question The main dispute CPL 40.20 is the section of New York’s Criminal Procedure Law that holds the double jeopardy rule, and part (2) of it comes with a list of exceptions. If one of them applies, the second prosecution is allowed even though the first two questions were both a yes. So this is where the prosecution gets its chance to keep the case, and it’s the main question being fought over. The exception that matters here has two parts, shown in the two cards inside this one, and the prosecution needs both of them. This is where the case is sitting right now. The judge hasn’t ruled on it. Both are needed and
Does each offense contain an element the other lacks?
The first part of the exception

Agreed by both sides This is the first part of the exception. An element is one of the things a prosecutor has to prove for a particular crime. This part asks if each of the two crimes needs something proven that the other one doesn’t, and it has to work in both directions. Second-degree murder needs proof that he meant to cause a death, and federal stalking plainly has no such requirement. The defense agreed in its motion that this part is met, so it isn’t where the fight is. The fight is in the other part.
Are the two statutes designed to prevent very different kinds of harm?
The second part of the exception

Undecided This is the second part, and it’s where the real fight is. It isn’t enough for the two crimes to be built differently on paper. The two laws also have to be aimed at very different kinds of harm. So the prosecution has to show that the federal stalking law and New York’s murder law exist to protect against different things, even though in this case both were charged over the same death. There’s a twist in it too. The strongest support for the prosecution’s side comes from the federal case itself, where the judge ruled in January 2026 that stalking isn’t a crime of violence. That was a ruling the defense asked for, and it’s what took the death penalty off the table.

Outcome Then Tried on counts three through ten If the judge finds the exception applies, double jeopardy doesn’t block the New York case and it goes ahead. He would be tried in front of a jury on the murder count and the seven weapons counts, even though he has already pleaded guilty in federal court over the same morning. There’s no date for that trial right now. It was supposed to start on September 8, 2026, but that date came and went while this motion was waiting to be decided, and no new one has been set.

Outcome Then Counts three through ten dismissed If no exception applies, New York’s double jeopardy law stops the state from prosecuting him over that morning a second time. The murder count is dismissed and all seven weapons counts go with it. That wouldn’t mean nothing happens to him. He would still be sentenced in the federal case in December, where each of the two counts he pleaded guilty to carries up to life. It would mean New York never puts him on trial for the killing at all.

Outside the motion, either way There’s one charge this whole fight doesn’t touch. Count eleven is for having a forged New Jersey driver’s license, and the indictment dates it to November 24, 2024, which is ten days before the killing. A different day and a different act means it isn’t part of the same criminal transaction the federal case covered, so double jeopardy has nothing to say about it. The defense didn’t even ask for it to be dismissed. So whichever way the judge rules above, this one count stays. If the defense wins everything it asked for, a fake driver’s license is all that would be left of the New York case.

Read as a whole, the case is a sequence of wins that each cost the winner something. The defense beat the terrorism counts, and in doing so reduced the state case to the one New York could most easily retry. It beat the capital counts, and in doing so established that the federal case is about stalking rather than violence — which is the premise the People now need. The District Attorney won the right to go first, and in doing so left the federal case idle and available to be closed by the defendant alone. None of those were mistakes. They were just moves in two games at once, scored in one.
Five days and some two hundred and eighty miles. Almost everything the rest of the case argues about was in a backpack in Altoona.

Brian Thompson, fifty years old and the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, is shot dead on the sidewalk outside a midtown Manhattan hotel, early in the morning, on his way into his company’s investor conference. He leaves a wife and two sons.

Luigi Mangione, twenty-six, is arrested in Altoona, Pennsylvania, after a customer recognizes him. Officers find a backpack. Inside it: a firearm fitted with a silencer, a loaded magazine, a forged New Jersey driver’s license, a passport, a phone, and a red spiral notebook of handwritten entries. Every item on that list is litigated in two courts over the following eighteen months, and the two courts do not agree. The order in which the officers looked in the bag — at the counter, or later at the station on an inventory form — is the whole of the dispute, and it is the kind of question that only gets asked because a federal court and a state court were both asking it.
Within eleven days he is a defendant in a state court, a federal court, and a Pennsylvania county court. Only one of those three ever gets near a jury.

A New York County grand jury returns murder in the first degree in furtherance of an act of terrorism, murder in the second degree as a crime of terrorism, murder in the second degree, seven weapons counts, and one count of possessing a forged instrument. Signed by District Attorney Alvin L. Bragg Jr. Counts one through ten are each pleaded as having happened “on or about December 4, 2024.” Count eleven is not: the forged New Jersey license is pleaded as “on or about November 24, 2024,” ten days before the killing. Nobody had reason to care about that difference for another twenty months. It is now the reason one count of this indictment is going to outlive the other ten whatever happens. Indictment, No. 75657-24 (N.Y. Cty. Sup. Ct.), counts 1–11

The United States charges him separately in the Southern District of New York: interstate stalking, stalking by electronic communication, murder through use of a firearm, and a firearm-and-silencer count. The first two are the ones that matter in the end; at this point they look like the small ones.

Brought to New York and presented in the federal court the same day. Detention on consent, without prejudice. He is held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, in federal custody, for the whole of what follows — which is why, later, a federal judge has to order that he be allowed a suit to wear to a state court hearing.
And a third prosecution, in Blair County

Pennsylvania charges him over the arrest itself: forgery and carrying a firearm without a license, both felonies, plus tampering with records, possessing an instrument of crime, and giving a false identification to police. It never moves. The federal courts decline repeatedly to produce him in Pennsylvania, citing cost and security; a hearing set for November 2025 is canceled when he will not appear remotely. A Blair County judge treats his unavailability as a waiver of Rule 600, Pennsylvania’s speedy-trial rule, and orders the case reported on every sixty days. It is still open and has never been tried. This page does not track it further.
For ten months the federal case is a death penalty case. It stops being one on a point of statutory construction that has nothing to do with what happened on West 54th Street.

Because the federal case is capital, the court appoints Avraham Moskowitz at public expense under 18 U.S.C. § 3005, alongside the retained team of Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan. The appointment is a reliable marker of what the case is: it arrives when the case becomes capital and it is withdrawn when it stops being one.
Moving to preclude a notice that has not been filed

The defense asks the court to bar the government from seeking death before the government has said it will. The motion is later denied as moot, without prejudice, once the notice actually arrives. ECF No. 16

Counts One and Two: stalking, by interstate travel and by electronic communication, each with death resulting, each carrying a maximum of life. Count Three: murder through use of a firearm, 18 U.S.C. § 924(j). Count Four: use of a firearm, brandished, discharged and silenced, § 924(c). Count Three is the only count in any of the three cases that could carry a death sentence. ECF No. 22
Notice of intent to seek the death penalty
Filed the day before the arraignment. ECF No. 25

Not guilty on all four counts. The court sets a motions schedule and says what it intends to do about the trial date, in terms the parties go on quoting back to it for the next year. “But my goal will be to leave that December 5 conference with a firm trial date set for 2026,” and “barring some request otherwise, my intention is that we will set a schedule for this case as if it’s the only case.” It was not the only case, and the second half of that sentence is what the fight over who goes first is about. 4/25/25 Tr. at 12, 17, quoted at ECF No. 108
The terrorism theory does not survive the first serious look at it, and with it goes any possibility of life without parole in New York.
The state omnibus motion — including double jeopardy, first time

The defense moves in state court to suppress the backpack and his statements, to bar identification testimony from witnesses who had grown familiar with surveillance footage, to dismiss the terrorism counts as unsupported by the grand jury evidence, and to dismiss the whole case on double jeopardy and constitutional grounds. Worth marking clearly, because it is the single most misreported thing about this case: the double jeopardy argument is not new, and it did not arrive with the plea. It was made here, in May 2025, and it lost. It lost because New York’s statute bars a second prosecution, and in May 2025 there had not yet been a first one that ended in anything. The argument was not wrong. It was early.
Carro, J.: the terrorism counts are legally insufficient

Counts one and two are dismissed. The court finds nothing in the grand jury record establishing the element the terrorism statutes require — an intent to intimidate a civilian population or to coerce a government. “There was no evidence presented that the defendant made any demands of government or sought any particular governmental policy change, let alone that he did so by intimidation or coercion.” The practical effect is a sentencing one. Murder in the first degree in New York carries life without parole; murder in the second degree carries twenty-five years to life, and is parole-eligible. From this date forward the state case is the less severe of the two in its maximum exposure — the federal stalking counts each carry life — which is worth holding onto, because it makes the plea eleven months later harder to read as simple damage control. Decision and order, Sept 16, 2025, Part 32
Moving to dismiss over what the Attorney General said

In the federal case, the defense moves to dismiss on the basis of public statements by senior Department of Justice officials, attaching a press release and an Instagram post by the Attorney General as exhibits. ECF No. 51, Exs. 1–2
Garnett, J. puts the Department of Justice on notice

The court finds that statements by two high-ranking Department staff, including within the Office of the Attorney General, “appear to be in direct violation” of Local Criminal Rule 23.1 and of its own April order, and orders a sworn declaration explaining how it happened. The order requires the declaration to come from “a person of suitable authority” — naming the Acting U.S. Attorney as the floor, “if not an official at Main Justice” — and directs the government to advise the Deputy Attorney General that future violations “may result in sanctions, which could include personal financial penalties, contempt of court findings, or relief specific to the prosecution of this matter,” and to confirm that the message was passed on. A declaration from the Acting U.S. Attorney follows on October 8. ECF No. 53; response and declaration at ECF No. 56

The motion that decides whether this is a death penalty case, and it is almost entirely technical. Counts Three and Four both require a predicate offense that is a crime of violence. The only predicate alleged is the federal stalking charged in Counts One and Two. The defense says stalking does not qualify. ECF No. 59
Days of testimony in Part 32 about the Altoona arrest. Partway through, the People withdraw his interrogation statements altogether, over a problem with Pennsylvania’s law on recording.
The federal case stops being capital, the two courts split on the backpack, and the District Attorney starts trying to get to a jury first. Everything after this follows from this month.
Oral argument on Counts Three and Four. The court also sets out the shape it has in mind for jury selection, with trial dates that depend on whether the case is still capital when it gets there.
The District Attorney asks to go first

Bragg’s office writes to Carro, J. asking for a state trial on July 1, 2026 — ahead of the federal case. New York has primary jurisdiction, having arrested him first, and the letter is the first open move in a fight about sequence that runs for the next six months.
A hearing about an inventory form

Garnett, J. orders the government to produce an Altoona police officer who can speak to the Department’s December 2024 procedures for securing and inventorying the property of someone arrested in a public place — adding that the witness “need not have had any personal involvement in the Defendant’s arrest,” because the question is about the procedure and not about him. ECF Nos. 90, 91

The first denies suppression of the backpack and everything in it. The second dismisses Counts Three and Four. Between them they take the death penalty off the table and leave the evidence in — and the reasoning in the second one is the reason the state case is now in trouble. On the backpack: suppression is denied on three independent grounds — the loaded magazine found in a pre-transport safety search, the rest recovered in an inventory search at the station, and in any event the inevitable discovery of all of it under the federal search warrant, “even excising references to any items found or seen after the magazine, firearm, and/or silencer were found.” On Counts Three and Four, the court is unusually direct about what it is being made to do. “The Court would be remiss not to note at the outset the apparent absurdity of the inquiry.” The defendant is charged with selecting a stranger to kill based on his employment, planning it, traveling across states to do it, and shooting him on a public street with a silenced handgun: “No one could seriously question that this is violent criminal conduct.” But the categorical approach forbids looking at the conduct, and asks instead about “the hypothetically least serious conduct that the charged crime could possibly cover.” Run that way, federal stalking fails twice over: the only element that could supply force can be committed recklessly, which is not enough, and the statute can be satisfied by a threat of self-harm, which is not force “against the person of another” at all. So stalking is not a crime of violence, so it cannot be the predicate, so Counts Three and Four go — and with them the only capital exposure anywhere in the case. “The analysis contained in the balance of this Opinion may strike the average person — and indeed many lawyers and judges — as tortured and strange, and the result may seem contrary to our intuitions about the criminal law. But it represents the Court’s committed effort to faithfully apply the dictates of the Supreme Court to the charges in this case. The law must be the Court’s only concern.” ECF Nos. 102 (backpack), 103 (Counts Three and Four)
Carro, J. moves the state trial up

The defense files the federal scheduling order in state court, showing Carro, J. that federal jury selection is set for September 8. He responds by moving the state trial forward, from a date in the fall to June 8, 2026. The defense then reports all of this back to the federal court, with an edge to it: the federal schedule had been set in open court and “extensively reported in the media,” and yet “the District Attorney’s Office did not write to Justice Carro or this Court at the time to address the state prosecutors’ concerns with a 2026 federal trial date. Given the above, the defense has been preparing for a federal trial.” ECF No. 108 and Ex. A

Being escorted out of a New York courtroom, Mangione is heard objecting to the prospect of back-to-back trials: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any common sense.” His counsel says double jeopardy is being used as a weapon against him. It is not a filing and it decides nothing, and it is on this page for one reason: it is an accurate statement of the constitutional position and an accurate statement of why that position loses. Under dual sovereignty, two prosecutions by two sovereigns are not the same offense, however much they look like the same trial. What saves the argument is not the Constitution but a New York statute, and the statute needs a conviction before it does anything.

Having been given a month to decide whether to take an interlocutory appeal of the dismissal, the government writes to say it will not. The federal case ceases to be capital for good. Learned counsel is relieved in April, with the court’s thanks. ECF Nos. 113, 114, 129
The race to go first, and who won it
Both trial dates move four times between them. In June the federal court yields and the state case gets what the District Attorney had asked for.
Both trials move, on the same day

The state trial is adjourned from June 8 to September 8, 2026. Hours later the federal court reshuffles its own schedule around that: in-person voir dire on October 13, openings on November 4, with January 2027 dates held in reserve “should a further adjournment of the trial become necessary.” ECF No. 124
Carro, J. splits the backpack the other way

The firearm and the red notebook are admissible, recovered under the Altoona Department’s own protocol. But what came out of the first search, at the counter in the McDonald’s, is suppressed — a loaded magazine, a passport, a wallet, a phone, a computer chip — because officers went into the bag without a warrant when he was already detained and surrounded. Pre-Miranda statements go too. So the two courts look at one backpack and give two answers. Garnett, J. denied suppression outright on January 30; Carro, J. grants it in part on May 18. Neither is obviously wrong — they are applying different records, and the federal ruling leans on a federal warrant the state case does not have — and nothing turns on the disagreement now that the federal case is over. It is here because it is the cleanest illustration of what running one killing through two systems actually produces: not a double punishment, but two different sets of facts. What survives in state court is also what matters most. Whatever the notebook is taken to show, it is in. Decision and order, May 18, 2026, Part 32

Garnett, J. adjourns the federal trial to January 25, 2027, with voir dire from January 5. The state case will go first, on September 8, by a clear four months. This is the posture that makes everything in August possible. It is worth stopping on this, because it is where the case turns and it does not look like it at the time. The District Attorney spent five months arguing for the right to try him first, and won. The consequence of winning is that on June 29 the federal case becomes the one that is not about to happen — and therefore the one that can be ended unilaterally, by a defendant, at a moment of his choosing, without anybody’s agreement. Six weeks later that is exactly what happens.
He pleads guilty in the case that was five months away, and the case that was three weeks away stops.
“I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died”

An open plea to Counts One and Two: guilty to both federal stalking counts, with no plea agreement, no charges dropped, and nothing conceded by the government in return. Maximum exposure, life. He tells the court he knew what he was doing was illegal. Sentencing is set for December 18, 2026, a presentence report ordered, detention continued. The timing is the whole of it. This is three and a half weeks before the state murder trial and five months before his own federal trial. He pleaded guilty, without consideration, in the case that was not about to start, and in doing so admitted on the record to the killing that the case about to start was going to be about. An open plea is normally a bad trade: the defendant surrenders the trial and receives nothing for it. It stops looking like a bad trade if what he is buying is not leniency but a conviction — because a conviction is the one thing New York’s double jeopardy statute needs before it can bar anything. That reading is an inference, not something either side has said on the record, and it is marked as an inference here. Change of plea, Aug 14, 2026; minute entry and oral order
And, within hours, a motion to end the state case

Filed the same day in Part 32: dismiss counts three through ten — the murder count and every weapons count — under New York’s double jeopardy statute and on due process grounds, together with a renewed suppression application. Counts three through ten, and not count eleven. The forged license is pleaded as November 24, 2024, and belongs to a different criminal transaction from the one the federal case covered, so there is nothing for the statute to bar. If the motion succeeds completely, what is left of this indictment is one count of carrying a fake New Jersey driver’s license. Karen Friedman Agnifilo, for the defense: “New York law does not permit a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime under a statute that covers successive prosecutions.” Motion to dismiss, Aug 14, 2026, Part 32
The state trial does not happen

Carro, J.’s order is three sentences long and never uses the word adjourned: the People respond by October 9, 2026, the defense may reply by October 30, and “the next adjourn date will be December 10, 2026.” The trial set for September 8 cannot go ahead while the motion is undecided, and so it simply does not. The People answer: a different evil

Forty-nine pages, filed for the District Attorney by Joel Seidemann. The weapons counts survive because the federal gun counts were dismissed before the plea. The murder count survives because stalking and murder are “designed to prevent very different kinds of harm or evil.” On the guns: in New York a case counts as an earlier prosecution of a charge only if it ends in a plea or a trial while that charge is still in it. “A mere charge is thus not enough to trigger double jeopardy,” and the federal firearm counts were gone by the time he pleaded. On murder, the brief turns the defense’s own federal win against it. In January the defense persuaded Garnett, J. that stalking is not a crime of violence, because a stalker need not intend or even foresee a death. The People say that is exactly why stalking aims at a different evil from murder: “The reasoning of that decision directly supports a finding that the requirements of CPL 40.20(2)(b) are satisfied here.” The due process claim is “nothing more than a masked double-jeopardy argument.” And the state-only defense the motion says he lost, extreme emotional disturbance, was in their view “doomed to fail” anyway: “The evidence in this case incontrovertibly establishes that this was a long-premeditated and well-choreographed killing.” People’s memorandum in opposition, Oct 9, 2026, at 1–3, 12, 21–23, 37
The defense replies: the same evil

Stalking a man with intent to kill him, and then killing him, is the same “core misconduct” as murder. And a gun count dropped from an indictment he pleaded to was still prosecuted. “One of the harms clearly addressed by the expansive federal stalking statute is stalking with the intent to kill and resulting in the killing of the person stalked,” Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan wrote. “It is a statute that, like a state murder statute, is intended to keep people safe from being murdered — the oldest crime there is.” The extra federal elements, crossing state lines and using electronics, “are not the evils or harms being prevented.” On the guns: “when Mangione pleaded guilty to the federal indictment, the criminal action in which he had been charged with possession and use of the firearm was terminated for statutory double jeopardy purposes.” It then takes the People’s cases one by one: “Every case allowing successive prosecution involved conduct that was different between the two prosecutions.” On due process it adds nothing, relying on the motion. The clerk stamped it received on November 2. Defense reply, Oct 30, 2026, at 2, 4–5, 9

Was he prosecuted in federal court for the gun?

People No. The two federal gun counts were thrown out in January, at his own request, more than six months before he pleaded. A charge that is gone before the plea was never “prosecuted,” so New York’s seven weapons counts can go ahead whatever happens to the murder count. Defense Yes. Under the statute he was prosecuted for anything charged in a case that ended in a guilty plea, and the federal case did. Nothing says he had to plead guilty to every count. The federal gun counts charged the same gun on the same morning as New York’s. Court Undecided. The motion is fully briefed, and Carro, J. has not ruled. The next appearance in Part 32 is December 10, 2026. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument New York’s law says a person “is prosecuted” for an offense when he “is charged therewith” and the case ends in a guilty plea. The People read the present tense literally: he has to still be charged with it when he pleads. “A mere charge is thus not enough to trigger double jeopardy.” They add that someone who gets a charge dismissed can be tried for it again, as long as the dismissal wasn’t a finding about guilt, and that a count that could never have led to a conviction never put him at risk at all. Rests on CPL 40.30(1), and the federal ruling of January 30, 2026, dismissing the two gun counts on his motion. People’s brief at 12–15 Authority Matter of Lockett v. Juviler, 65 N.Y.2d 182 (1985) (“an accused must suffer jeopardy … before he can suffer double jeopardy”); People v. Nuccio, 78 N.Y.2d 102 (1991); People v. Key, 45 N.Y.2d 111 (1978); People v. Aleynikov (Sup. Ct. N.Y. Cty. 2013). Where it is weak The statute also says the action has to end in a plea, and this one did. The case closest to these facts that the People cite, Aleynikov, is a trial-court decision, not a ruling that binds this court. Defense The argument The statute asks only two things: that he was charged in a filed accusation, and that “the action” ended in a guilty plea. “[T]here is no requirement that the defendant plead guilty to every specific offense.” The federal gun counts and the state weapons counts are about one gun, the one in his backpack in Altoona, used that morning. In reply: “The statutory definition of being ‘prosecuted’ for an offense does not require that the defendant plead guilty to that specific offense.” Rests on CPL 40.30(1)(a); counts three and four of the federal indictment. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 57–60, 78 · Defense reply at 2–3 Authority The words of the statute. The motion cites no case on this point, and the People point that out. Where it is weak He is relying on counts he asked the federal court to throw out, and won. On the defense reading, a count dismissed at any stage would still block a state charge, so long as something else in the case later ended in a plea. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Was he still “charged” with the federal gun counts when the case ended in his plea? People No. They were dismissed in January. By August 14 they were gone. People The words “is charged” mean charged at the time of the plea. Defense What has to end in a plea is the action, and the action did. Defense Same gun, same morning, charged by both governments. Where it lands Undecided. If the People are right, the seven weapons counts are tried whatever happens to the murder count. If the defense is right, the People’s brief gives no other reason to keep them.
Are federal stalking and New York murder aimed at very different harms?

People Yes. As written, the stalking law is about crossing state lines or using electronics to frighten someone. Nothing in its definition needs a death or an intent to kill. The murder law is about intending to kill and killing. In the brief’s words, “different harms, different evils, different purposes, different crimes.” Defense No. Both laws exist to punish the unlawful taking of a life. He pleaded guilty to stalking that ended in a death, which carries life in prison. The travel and electronics “are not the evils or harms being prevented.” Court Undecided, and this is the heart of the motion. Both sides agree that each crime has an element the other lacks, which is the first half of the exception. Everything turns on this second half. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument The court has to compare the laws as written, not what he did. Written that way, everything in federal stalking is missing from murder: travel or an electronic “course of conduct,” an intent to “kill, injure, harass, or intimidate,” and a victim placed in reasonable fear. A murder can happen to someone who never saw it coming, and federal stalking can happen without anyone dying. The defense itself told the federal court that “the central purpose of the stalking statutes at issue here is to protect that person who is stalked [from] emotional distress or … reasonable fear.” The life sentence it points to sits in a separate penalty section, and many federal crimes carry life with nobody killed. Rests on 18 U.S.C. § 2261A, the stalking law; Penal Law § 125.25(1), the murder law; the defense’s own federal brief, ECF No. 76. People’s brief at 15–21 Authority Matter of Kaplan v. Ritter, 71 N.Y.2d 222 (1987), on reading the laws and not the acts; People v. Bryant, 92 N.Y.2d 216 (1998); Matter of Robinson v. Snyder, 259 A.D.2d 280 (1st Dep’t 1999). Where it is weak The stalking law’s own list of intents starts with “kill,” and the counts he pleaded to were charged as stalking with intent to kill that ended in a death. Reading the laws “in the abstract” asks the court to look past that. Defense The argument The bar is high. The law needs “very” different harms, and slight differences don’t count. When two laws both aim at “punishment for the unlawful taking of a particular human life,” the exception fails. Read with its penalty section, the stalking law punishes a death that results with “life or any terms of years,” the same as the federal murder count that was dismissed. And, the defense says, the federal government will ask for his sentence to be figured from the guideline for first-degree murder. In reply: “It is a statute that, like a state murder statute, is intended to keep people safe from being murdered — the oldest crime there is.” The travel, the electronics and the victim’s fear are “peripheral distinctions that do not go to the heart of the conduct being punished.” Rests on 18 U.S.C. §§ 2261A and 2261(b)(1); the federal sentencing guidelines. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 62–72 · Defense reply at 4–6 Authority Matter of Wiley v. Altman, 52 N.Y.2d 410 (1981); Kaplan v. Ritter; People v. Manafort (Sup. Ct. N.Y. Cty. 2019). Where it is weak Its strongest material is in the penalty section and the sentencing guidelines, not in the definition of the crime, and the definition is what the court is told to compare. The People call that a single narrow overlap. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Were the two laws “designed to prevent very different kinds of harm or evil”? Judged by the laws as written, not by what he did. People Stalking’s elements are about fear and how it’s spread. Murder’s are about an intended death. People The death sits in a separate penalty section, not in the crime itself. Defense Read with its penalty, the stalking law punishes taking a life with life in prison. Defense Stalking someone with intent to kill, ending in his death, is the same “core misconduct” as murder. Where it lands Undecided, and it settles the murder count. If the People are right, he can be tried for murder in New York. If not, the murder count is dismissed.
What does the January ruling that stalking is not a crime of violence prove?

People That stalking and murder aim at different harms. The federal judge read the stalking law as written, the way New York’s test does, and found it needs no intent to cause a death and no use of force. The defense won that ruling by telling her the stalking law protects against fear. Defense Nothing about this question. “Crime of violence” is a narrow federal label. The ruling decided whether two federal counts could stand, not what the stalking law is for. Arson, kidnapping and even first-degree murder have failed the same test. Court Undecided. The motion is fully briefed, and Carro, J. has not ruled. The next appearance in Part 32 is December 10, 2026. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument The federal categorical approach ignores the facts and reads only the statute, which “parallels the ‘harm or evil’ inquiry” New York uses. Under it, Garnett, J. found that a stalker “need not intend or even know” the victim will be put in fear, and that a death “need not be foreseeable.” Her examples, like alarming messages that send a victim driving to a police station into a fatal crash, “bear no resemblance to the essential characteristics of second-degree murder.” The defense gave the federal court examples of its own like that. However “absurd” the inquiry is as a matter of federal law, the People say, it is the right one here. Rests on United States v. Mangione, 818 F. Supp. 3d 509 (S.D.N.Y. 2026), the January 30 ruling; the defense’s federal brief, ECF No. 76. People’s brief at 21–23 Authority Kaplan v. Ritter, 71 N.Y.2d at 229, which the People set beside the federal method. Where it is weak The two tests ask different things. The federal one asks whether a crime always involves force. New York’s asks what harm a law was written to prevent. A law can aim at preventing killings without force being one of its elements. Defense The argument Garnett, J. was deciding whether two federal counts met their elements, not “defining the purpose of the federal stalking statute or what harm it was meant to prevent.” A crime can fail the crime-of-violence test and still be aimed at violence. She said so herself, calling the question an “apparent absurdity” and writing that “No one could seriously question that this is violent criminal conduct.” In reply: another federal judge found federal first-degree murder isn’t a crime of violence either, so by the People’s logic federal and state murder laws would aim at very different harms. “That cannot be.” Rests on The same January 30 ruling, at 515–16. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 73–77 · Defense reply at 6–7 Authority United States v. Ahemeid, 819 F. Supp. 3d 143 (E.D.N.Y. 2026), first-degree murder; United States v. Walker, 934 F.3d 375 (4th Cir. 2019), kidnapping; United States v. Lung’aho, 72 F.4th 845 (8th Cir. 2023), arson. Where it is weak The People are quoting the defense’s own January argument back at it: that the stalking law’s central purpose is protecting people from fear. The defense needed that to be true to take the death penalty off the table. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Does a federal ruling on what counts as a crime of violence tell a New York court what harm the stalking law was meant to prevent? People Both tests read the law, not the facts, so the answer carries over. People The ruling shows stalking needs neither an intent to kill nor force. Defense A crime can fail the federal test and still be aimed at violence. Murder has. Defense The ruling was about two federal counts, not about what the law is for. Where it lands Undecided. It’s the People’s strongest support, and it’s a ruling the defense asked for.
Which earlier cases is this one like?

People Cases where one episode broke two laws aimed at different things, and both prosecutions went ahead. A burglary and the stolen goods from it. A federal bank robbery and a state attempted murder of a police officer. The defense’s case was a conspiracy to murder, which holds the whole murder inside it. Defense Wiley v. Altman. A man prosecuted in Maryland for conspiring to commit a murder could not then be tried in New York for the murder, because both laws aimed at “the unlawful taking of a particular human life.” Where the harms are “generally similar,” the exception does not apply. Court Undecided. The motion is fully briefed, and Carro, J. has not ruled. The next appearance in Part 32 is December 10, 2026. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument In People v. Lanahan the court let burglary and possessing stolen property both go ahead over one theft, because burglary protects “the integrity of a residence.” Courts have refused only where the laws overlapped far more, like two boating-safety rules. Wiley involved a conspiracy that carried every element of the murder inside it, and the People say the law was later changed in response. Manafort involved state and federal fraud laws both written after the 2008 financial crisis, and nothing like that connects stalking and murder. The stalking law’s history points the same way. It started in the 1994 Violence Against Women Act, aimed at abusers who crossed state lines, then grew in 1996 to cover celebrity-style stalking of strangers, and later the internet. Every step was about fear. Rests on The legislative history of 18 U.S.C. § 2261A, from 1994 to 2013. People’s brief at 24–31 Authority People v. Lanahan, 276 A.D.2d 906 (3d Dep’t 2000); People v. Bryant, 92 N.Y.2d 216 (1998); Matter of McNerlin v. Argento, 173 A.D.3d 1646 (4th Dep’t 2019); People v. Claud, 76 N.Y.2d 951 (1990), the other way. Where it is weak The defense’s reply answers each one: in every case the People cite, the victim, the place, the time or the conduct differed between the two prosecutions. Here none of them does. Defense The argument In Wiley the Maryland charge was conspiracy, not murder, but it allowed the same punishment as the murder it aimed at, life in prison. The Court of Appeals held both prosecutions “were directed at a like goal; punishment for the unlawful taking of a particular human life.” The same is true here: stalking that results in death also carries life. In Manafort, the court held the exception requires “a significant and meaningful difference in the types of harms addressed.” In reply it takes the People’s cases one by one. Lanahan’s burglaries happened on other nights in other places, and in Claud two quite different boating laws still counted as aimed at the same harm. “Every case allowing successive prosecution involved conduct that was different between the two prosecutions.” Rests on The Court of Appeals’ reasoning in Wiley, and Manafort, attached to the motion as Exhibit A. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 63–68 · Defense reply at 7–9 Authority Matter of Wiley v. Altman, 52 N.Y.2d 410 (1981); People v. Manafort (Sup. Ct. N.Y. Cty. 2019), affirmed, 187 A.D.3d 612 (1st Dep’t 2020); People v. Claud, 76 N.Y.2d 951 (1990), read the other way. Where it is weak Wiley leaned on what a conspiracy is. It takes in every act of the crime it aims at, so the overlap was nearly total. Stalking, the People say, does not take in a murder that way. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test In the closest past cases, did New York let the second prosecution go ahead? People Yes, whenever the two laws had different aims, even over one theft or one shooting. People Wiley was a conspiracy, which holds the whole murder inside it. Stalking doesn’t. Defense In Wiley both laws punished one taking of a life with life in prison. So do these. Defense The harms only need to be generally similar for the exception to fail. Where it lands Undecided. Neither side cites an earlier case that put federal stalking beside state murder, so the court has to choose which line of cases this belongs to.
Did the District Attorney already admit the plea would end the case?

People No. In February a prosecutor said the defense was delaying “hoping” the state case would be “jeopardied out” if the federal case went first. That describes the defense’s plan. It doesn’t agree the plan would work. Defense In effect, yes. For months the office pressed to go first because, in its own words, the defense was trying to “jeopardy [the state] out of the case.” In July it wrote that a federal plea “would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution.” Court Undecided. The motion is fully briefed, and Carro, J. has not ruled. The next appearance in Part 32 is December 10, 2026. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument The defense quotes the February 6 transcript as an admission. The full sentence, the People say, was that the defense was trying to delay the state case “hoping that if it goes after the federal case, by the New York statutory double jeopardy[, the state case] would be jeopardied out” (emphasis on “hoping” theirs). In June the prosecutor “simply pointed out that the defense was transparently seeking to manipulate the court’s calendar in order to manufacture a statutory double-jeopardy claim.” None of it was “anything like a concession.” Rests on The minutes of February 6 and June 3, 2026, attached to the People’s affirmation. People’s brief at 31–32 Authority None needed. It’s a question of what was said. Where it is weak The office fought hard and openly to try the case first. Whatever its prosecutors believed about the law, the effort makes most sense if they thought going second could cost them the case. Defense The argument On February 6 the office argued the defense was trying to “jeopardy [the state] out of the case,” and the judge moved the trial up to June 8, saying the federal government had “reneged on their agreement to allow the state that did most of the work in this case to go first.” On June 3 defense counsel said the People were “desperate” to go first, and the office didn’t dispute it. On July 2 it wrote that a federal plea “would operate to defeat a just outcome in the state prosecution.” Rests on The transcripts of February 6 and June 3, 2026, and the People’s letter of July 2, 2026. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 28–34 Authority None needed. It’s a question of what was said. Where it is weak A prosecutor worrying that a defense might work is not the same as agreeing that it does. And even a real concession on the law wouldn’t bind the judge, who has to decide the statute’s meaning for himself. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did anything the District Attorney’s office said amount to agreeing that a federal plea bars the state case? People No. Its prosecutors described what the defense was hoping for and objected to it. People Describing the defense’s plan isn’t endorsing it. Defense An office doesn’t race to go first unless it thinks going second loses. Defense Its own letter said a federal plea would defeat the state case. Where it lands Undecided, and probably not decisive. What the statute means is the judge’s question, whatever either side said along the way.
Did the two prosecutions together deny him due process?

People No. Two governments may each prosecute the same act, and their prosecutors may talk about scheduling. The state went first on its own timetable. The defense it says he lost was extreme emotional disturbance, which was “doomed to fail” anyway, and he withdrew it himself. Defense Yes. The two offices “cut a deal” for the state to go first. That forced a choice: raise a defense that exists only in New York and admit facts the federal prosecutors would use, or give it up. Acting together, they were a single government trying him twice. Court Undecided. The motion is fully briefed, and Carro, J. has not ruled. The next appearance in Part 32 is December 10, 2026. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak People The argument The claim is “nothing more than a masked double-jeopardy argument.” A due process claim needs either unfair procedure or conduct that “shock[s] the contemporary conscience,” and talking about scheduling is neither. The Justice Department’s long-standing “Petite” policy tells federal prosecutors to weigh a state case already underway. In April 2025 the federal prosecutor told his court that his office would proceed “in our normal course.” In June 2026 the judge only warned that, without a proper notice, the defense was “coming close to not being able to put forth” extreme emotional disturbance, and the defense withdrew its notice instead of fixing it. “The evidence in this case incontrovertibly establishes that this was a long-premeditated and well-choreographed killing.” If he regrets his federal plea, that is for the federal court. Rests on The People’s affirmation of October 9 and its exhibits: minutes of April 25, 2025, and January 9, January 30 and June 17, 2026. People’s brief at 32–40 Authority Reed v. Goertz, 598 U.S. 230 (2023); Charles v. Orange County, 925 F.3d 73 (2d Cir. 2019); United States v. Aboumoussallem, 726 F.2d 906 (2d Cir. 1984); People v. Harrison, 212 A.D.3d 651 (2d Dep’t 2023). Where it is weak Its answer that the defense was “doomed to fail” is the People’s own view of a defense no court has heard. And the defense quotes the state court itself moving the trial up because the federal government had “reneged” on an agreement about who would go first. Defense The argument “In a word, the District Attorney’s Office and the Justice Department cut a deal.” Because the state went first, he faced “an intractable constitutional dilemma”: to use the defense New York offers, which can reduce murder to manslaughter, he would have had to admit facts the federal prosecutors would use to convict him, and the court required him to lay out that defense in detail before trial. “We are unaware of a single other case with this combination of circumstances in the history of prosecutions in this country.” The reply adds nothing on due process: it “relies on the arguments made in Mangione’s opening brief.” Rests on The scheduling record from January to June 2026; a federal press release of December 19, 2024, thanking the state office for its “separate prosecution” expected to go first. Defense affirmation ¶¶ 39–47 · Defense reply at 9 Authority Snyder v. Massachusetts, 291 U.S. 97 (1934); Lisenba v. California, 314 U.S. 219 (1941); Patterson v. New York, 432 U.S. 197 (1977). The motion invokes the Fifth Amendment; the People say the Fourteenth is the one that applies to a state.
